title: The same water, two peoples
sum: Chapter 10 ended with Wisdom leading Israel through the sea. Chapter 11 carries her guidance into the desert (11:1–4), then turns the story into a prayer to God and states the rule of the rest of the book: "The very things that punished their enemies / were the things that did them good" (11:5). The first contrast follows: Egypt's Nile turned to blood as a rebuke for drowning Israel's babies, while Israel drank water from the rock (11:6–14).

At 11:15 the writer starts a long digression. Egypt worshiped animals, so it was punished by animals (11:15–16). God could have sent monsters, but he set everything "by measure, by number and by weight" (11:20). And his restraint is not weakness but love: "You love all that is" (11:24), "Master, lover of souls" (11:26).
readings: Read as a retelling of Exodus

The writer chooses scenes from Exodus and Numbers and arranges them in pairs, Egypt against Israel. He leaves out names and leaves out Israel's complaining, so that the wilderness becomes a model of God's care. Jewish interpreters of the time often retold Scripture this way, filling gaps and drawing lessons.
Read as theology of God's mercy

The second half of the chapter is among the most quoted passages of the book. God's power, which could crush the world like a speck on a scale, is the very reason for his patience. God hates nothing he has made, and he overlooks sins to bring people to repentance (11:23–24).

views.C: Catholic Bibles include Wisdom of Solomon in the Old Testament. The Lectionary reads 11:22–12:2 on the 31st Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year C, with Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1–10), the rich man whom Jesus seeks out: God loves all he has made and corrects sinners little by little. Augustine's use of 11:20, "measure, number and weight", made the line a favorite of Catholic thought on the order of creation (City of God 11.30).
views.O: The Orthodox Old Testament, which follows the Septuagint, includes the book. Orthodox readers hear in 11:24–26 the language of their own prayers, which often call God the lover of humankind, and in 11:4 the rock that Paul calls Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
views.P: Protestant churches do not count the book as Scripture (see the book's introduction), but many readers value its teaching that God's patience aims at repentance, which agrees with Romans 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9. They note that Exodus says nothing of Israel's "prayer" at the rock; the Bible stresses the people's complaining (Exodus 17:3; Numbers 20:2).
views.H: Scholars call chapters 11–19 a series of comparisons (in Greek rhetoric, synkrisis) between Egypt and Israel, built on the rule of 11:5 and broken by two digressions (11:15–12:27; 13:1–15:17). Phrases such as "formless matter" (11:17) and God's spirit in all things (12:1) show a writer at home in Greek philosophy, writing for Jews of Egypt.
views.J: The rule that the punishment fits the sin (11:16) is one the rabbis also taught: "With the measure that a person measures, he is measured with it" (Mishnah Sotah 1:7). Linking the blood of the Nile to Pharaoh's decree (11:7) is found in later Jewish interpretation as well. The book itself was kept by Greek-speaking Christians, not in the Jewish Bible.

deep.b: From 11:1 to the end, the book compares what God did to Egypt and to Israel. Scholars usually count seven pairs: (1) Egypt's river of blood, Israel's water from the rock (11:6–14); (2) animals that tormented Egypt, quails that fed Israel (16:1–4); (3) insects that killed Egyptians, the bronze snake that healed Israel (16:5–14); (4) hail and fire that ruined Egypt's crops, manna that fell for Israel (16:15–29); (5) darkness for Egypt, the pillar of fire for Israel (17:1–18:4); (6) the death of Egypt's firstborn, Israel spared (18:5–25); (7) the sea that drowned Egypt and let Israel pass (19:1–9). The rule behind them all is 11:5. Between the first and second pairs stand the two great digressions: on God's mercy (11:15–12:27) and on false worship (13:1–15:17), which this part of the book contains.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why the digression comes here
deep.b: The rule of 11:5 raises an objection at once: if God could punish Egypt with its own gods, why so slowly, plague after plague? I suggest the digression on mercy (11:15–12:27) answers exactly that objection before the reader can make it. Its key words are "a little at a time" (12:2; 12:8; 12:10), and it uses the Canaanites as a second test case. This fits Exodus 23:29–30 and Deuteronomy 7:22, which also say the nations were removed "bit by bit". The point overlaps with what commentators call the book's theodicy (its defense of God's justice), but the link to the slow pace of the plagues as the trigger for the digression is my own reading.

echoes: Exodus 1:22; Exodus 2:3; Exodus 7:20–21; Exodus 8:2–6; Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11; Deuteronomy 8:15; Isaiah 40:15; Psalm 114:8; Matthew 7:2; Acts 17:30; Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9; 2 Maccabees 7:28; 1 Corinthians 10:4

settings.what: The desert and the first contrast: water
settings.by: the book's speaker, in the voice of Solomon (7:1), who turns at 11:4 from telling about Wisdom to speaking to God
settings.to: God, in prayer; the book's readers listen in
settings.when: a retelling of Israel's journey through the wilderness after the Exodus (Exodus 15–17; Numbers 20)
settings.why: To show that the same part of creation that punished Egypt saved Israel, and so to give a rule for reading the whole Exodus story (11:5).
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. For them Egypt was not a distant past but the land they lived in. The story told them that the God who had judged Egypt still cared for his people there.
views: Most readers take the retelling as encouragement to a minority: God has always protected his people against stronger neighbors.
Others stress the warning to Jews drawn to the gods and ways of Egypt and Greece: the Egyptians were punished by what they worshiped.

settings.what: Digression on God's power and mercy
settings.when: between the first contrast (water) and the second (animals, 16:1–4)
settings.why: To answer why the all-powerful God punished Egypt and Canaan slowly and gently: he loves what he made, and he gives time for repentance. The lesson is for Israel too: the righteous must be kind to all (12:19).
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. Living among the descendants of Israel's old enemies, they are taught to hope for mercy and to show it (12:22).
views: The passage is a reflection on God's character, with Egypt and Canaan as examples.
It also answers critics who found the plagues and the conquest cruel, by showing that God gave the nations time.

title: Room to repent
sum: The digression on mercy goes on. God's imperishable spirit is in all things, so he corrects sinners a little at a time (12:1–2). The writer's great test case is Canaan. Its people did terrible things: sorcery, child sacrifice, cannibal feasts (12:3–6). Yet God sent wasps ahead of Israel's army to remove them slowly, giving them "room for repentance" (12:8–10), though he knew they would not change.

No one can call God to account (12:12–14), and his power is the very source of his righteousness and his sparing (12:15–18). From this, Israel learns that "whoever is righteous must love people" (12:19), and that if God was so careful with enemies, he will judge his own children with mercy (12:20–22). The chapter closes back in Egypt, where people worshiped despised animals and were mocked, then judged, by them (12:23–27).
readings: Read as an answer to the conquest

This is one of the earliest Jewish reflections on the moral problem of the conquest of Canaan. Its answer: the Canaanites' guilt was real, but God was patient and gave them time; the slowness of the conquest (Exodus 23:29–30) was mercy.
Read as a lesson for Israel
The chapter is finally about Israel. Its people are to learn kindness from God's way with enemies, and to hope for mercy when they themselves are judged (12:19–22).

views.C: The Lectionary reads 12:13 and 12:16–19 on the 16th Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year A, with the parable of the weeds and the wheat (Matthew 13:24–30), where the master lets both grow until harvest. Catholic readers take the chapter as a witness to God's patience and his desire that sinners repent (Ezekiel 18:23).
views.O: Orthodox readers, with the Fathers, emphasize God's love for humankind (12:19) and his giving of "room for repentance", a phrase they know from Hebrews 12:17.
views.P: Protestants do not read the book as Scripture, but the chapter's themes are biblical: God's patience (Romans 2:4), the Amorites' guilt filling up over time (Genesis 15:16), and the Lord's discipline of his children (Hebrews 12:5–11). Many would question 12:10–11, that a whole people's evil was "born in them".
views.H: Historians note the Greek coloring of the charges against Canaan: "initiates" and a frenzied cult band (12:5) belong to the language of Greek mystery religions. The writer reads the Torah through the eyes of Alexandria, where such cults were known.
views.J: The idea that God judged Canaan only when its sins were complete has roots in Genesis 15:16 and Leviticus 18:24–28. Jewish writers of the Greek period also defended Israel's claim to the land against Greek critics; this chapter is one such defense, addressed to God.

deep.b: Wisdom of Solomon gives a three-part answer. (1) The Canaanites' crimes were grave: sorcery, child sacrifice, cannibal feasts (12:3–6), the sins the Torah also names (Deuteronomy 18:9–12; Leviticus 18:21–25). (2) God was patient: he sent wasps to drive them out "a little at a time", giving room to repent (12:8–10). (3) No one can accuse God, because he alone cares for all and has no rival to answer to (12:12–14). Readers today ask harder questions than the writer did, and the holy-war topic sets out the range of answers. The book's answer stands out for one thing: it insists that God loved even these enemies "since they were human" (12:8).

echoes: Genesis 9:25; Genesis 15:16; Exodus 23:28–30; Leviticus 18:21–25; Deuteronomy 7:20–22; Deuteronomy 18:9–12; Joshua 24:12; Job 9:12; Romans 2:4; Romans 9:20; Hebrews 12:5–11; Hebrews 12:17; Matthew 13:24–30

title: The Maker seen in what he made
sum: Now the writer begins his second digression, on false worship (13:1–15:17). First come the more respectable errors. Some people saw the beauty and power of fire, wind, stars and water and took them for gods. They should have reasoned from the works to the Craftsman: "From how great and how beautiful created things are, / their Maker is seen, by analogy" (13:5). They deserve little blame, since they were seeking God (13:6–7), yet they cannot be excused, because minds that could explore the universe could have found its Master (13:8–9).

Then come the idol-makers, who are "miserable" (13:10). In a satire built on Isaiah 44, a woodcutter uses good wood for furniture, scraps for his cooking fire, and the worst knotty piece, carved in his spare time, for a god. He paints it, nails it to the wall so it will not fall, and prays to it for health, life and success (13:11–19).
readings: Read as natural theology

The first nine verses are the Greek Old Testament's fullest argument that God can be known from creation. They stand behind Romans 1:19–25 and have been cited by Catholic and Orthodox teaching ever since (Catechism 32 and 41; John of Damascus, Exact Exposition 1.1).
Read as satire
The second half is comedy with a point, in the line of Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10: a god made from leftover scraps, propped up so it will not fall, asked for the very things it most lacks.

views.C: Catholic teaching leans on this chapter with Romans 1. The Catechism cites 13:1–9 beside Romans 1:19–20 for the "proofs" of God from the world's order and beauty (Catechism 32) and quotes 13:5 for naming God from creatures (Catechism 41). Vatican I taught that God can be known with certainty from created things (Dei Filius, chapter 2). The weekday Lectionary reads 13:1–9 on Friday of the 32nd week in Ordinary Time, Year 1.
views.O: John of Damascus cites 13:5 at the start of his Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith (1.1): creation and its order "proclaim the majesty of the Divine nature". He goes on to argue for God's existence from change and order (1.3), while holding that God's essence cannot be known (1.4). See the card below.
views.P: Protestants read the chapter mainly through Romans 1, which they hold as Scripture. Calvin taught that God's glory is engraved on all his works but that, because of sin, creation's witness leaves people without excuse rather than leading them to God (Institutes 1.5). Karl Barth rejected natural theology outright. See the card below and the card at Romans 1.
views.H: The argument from design was well known to Greek philosophers, the Stoics above all, and the writer turns it against Greek religion itself: if the world is so beautiful, its Maker is more beautiful still. Most scholars think Paul in Romans 1:18–32 draws on this chapter or on the synagogue teaching it records.
views.J: Philo of Alexandria makes the same charge against those who worship the elements and the heavens (On the Decalogue 52–66), and the Torah warns Israel not to bow to the sun, moon and stars (Deuteronomy 4:19). The satire on idols continues Isaiah 44:9–20 and Jeremiah 10:1–16.

deep.h: Wisdom 13 and Romans 1, step by step
deep.b:
(1) God can be known from his works: Wisdom 13:1–5; Romans 1:19–20. (2) People are without excuse: "even they are not to be excused" (13:8); "This leaves them with no defense" (Romans 1:20). (3) They turned to creatures and images: 13:2, 13:10–14:21; "an image of mortal man, of birds, of four-footed animals and of crawling things" (Romans 1:23); "They revered and served the created thing rather than the One who created it" (Romans 1:25). (4) False worship leads to sexual sin and every vice: 14:12, 14:22–27; Romans 1:24–31. Paul then turns on the reader who judges (Romans 2:1), where Wisdom of Solomon turns to "But you, our God" and "we are yours" (15:1–2).

There is one difference worth noticing. Wisdom 13:6 says the nature-worshipers deserve "small" blame, since they were seeking God; Paul says they "hold down the truth by their unrighteousness" (Romans 1:18). See the notes at 13:5 and at Romans 1:20.

echoes: Exodus 3:14; Genesis 1:14; Deuteronomy 4:19; Psalm 19:1–4; Psalm 115:4–8; Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Acts 14:15–17; Acts 17:24–29; Romans 1:18–25; Hebrews 11:10

settings.to: no one directly: the speaker talks about the nations to the book's readers, before returning to address God in 14:3
settings.when: the start of the second digression (13:1–15:17), after the rebuke of Egypt's animal worship (12:23–27)
settings.why: To show that even the best pagan religion, the worship of nature, is a failure to reason from the works to their Maker, and so to strengthen readers who lived among educated Greeks.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. Some of their neighbors were philosophers who called the elements or the world divine; the writer uses their own argument from beauty and order against them.
views: Many read it as a Jewish answer to Greek philosophy, aimed at educated readers.
Others think it was mainly meant to steady Jews themselves against the attraction of Greek religion.

settings.to: the readers, with prayers to God at 14:3–6 and 15:1–6
settings.when: the center of the second digression
settings.why: To mock the making of idols, to explain how idolatry began (14:12–21) and what it leads to (14:22–31), and to set Israel's God and Israel's worship against it (15:1–6).
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. Alexandria was full of temples, statues of gods and images of the Ptolemies; the chapter gave Jews arguments for refusing to honor them.
views: The tone is mocking, in the tradition of Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115.
The account of how idols began (14:12–21) is also an early attempt to explain the origin of religion, using a Greek theory.

traditions.q: Wisdom 13:5 says the Maker "is seen, by analogy" from the greatness and beauty of what he made. Is there a real likeness between creatures and God, so that the mind can argue from the world to its Maker? (Whether people can know God from creation at all is asked on the card at Romans 1.)
views: Yes, with a strict limit. The First Vatican Council taught that God "can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things" by the natural light of human reason (Dei Filius, chapter 2 and canon 2.1). The Catechism cites this verse: the perfections of creatures reflect God's, so we can name God from them (Catechism 41). But it adds, from the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), that "between Creator and creature no similitude can be expressed without implying an even greater dissimilitude" (Catechism 43). Thomas Aquinas holds that God's existence can be shown from his effects (Summa Theologiae I, question 2, articles 2–3) and that words are said of God and creatures "in an analogous sense, i.e. according to proportion" (I, question 13, article 5).

Yes for God's existence, no for his essence. John of Damascus cites this verse at the start of his Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith and says that knowledge of God's existence "has been implanted by Him in all by nature" (1.1). He argues from change and from the order of the world that there is a God (1.3), but says that "what He is in His essence and nature is absolutely incomprehensible and unknowable" (1.4).

Reasoning from creation does not reach the God who saves. Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518) says that the one who looks on God's invisible things "as though they were clearly perceptible in those things which have actually happened" does not deserve to be called a theologian, and that the true theologian sees God's visible things "through suffering and the cross" (theses 19–20). Thesis 19 has Paul's words about God's invisible things in view.

Reformed teachers differ on how much the likeness can do. Calvin says God's glory is engraved on each of his works, though "His essence, indeed, is incomprehensible" (Institutes 1.5.1); yet "In vain for us, therefore, does Creation exhibit so many bright lamps" (1.5.14), since sin blinds us, and the witness serves to leave us without excuse (1.5.15). Karl Barth went further and rejected the Catholic "analogy of being" as a ground for knowing God, writing in the preface to his Church Dogmatics I/1, against the Catholic thinker Erich Przywara: "I regard the analogia entis as the invention of Antichrist".

title: Blessed wood and cursed wood
sum: The sailor about to cross a wild sea prays to a piece of wood more rotten than his ship, though it is God's providence that steers every ship (14:1–5). So it was in the Flood, when the hope of the world fled onto a raft (14:6). "For blessed is wood through which righteousness comes about" (14:7), but the idol and its maker are cursed (14:8–11).

The writer then tells how idols began. A father, mad with grief, made an image of his dead child and honored it as a god; the custom became law. People far from their king made his image and flattered it, and an artist's skill turned admiration into worship (14:12–21). The result is a world at war that calls itself peace: secret rites, child sacrifice, murder, adultery, perjury, a whole catalog of vices, for idolatry is "the start of every evil" (14:22–31).
readings: Read as a history of religion

The chapter offers two origins for idolatry: grief for the dead (14:15) and the worship of rulers (14:17–20). Both follow Greek theories about how gods began, and both point to human feeling, not to real gods, as the source.
Read as Christian figure
Christian readers heard 14:7 of the cross, the wood through which righteousness comes, against the cursed idol of 14:8 (see the notes at 14:7).

views.C: Thomas Aquinas cites 14:21, "the incommunicable name", to show that the name "God" belongs properly to God alone (Summa Theologiae I, question 13, article 9). Catholic readers have applied 14:7 to the cross, and the chapter's vice list has long been compared with Romans 1:29–31.
views.O: John of Damascus, in his defense of the holy images, quotes a bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus who cites 14:7 for the honor given to the cross. The Orthodox distinguish the honor given to icons from the worship condemned here: an idol is called a god (14:8), an icon is not.
views.P: Reformed Protestants have read the attack on images as support for their teaching against images in worship; see the card at Deuteronomy 4 for the churches' views. Many Protestants also note that the vice list follows the same order as Romans 1: idols, then sexual sin, then every kind of wrong.
views.H: The account of the grieving father follows Euhemerus' theory that gods were once humans (about 300 BC), and the account of royal images reflects the ruler cult of the Ptolemies and, later, of Rome. Some scholars use 14:16–20 to date the book to the early Roman Empire, under Augustus or Caligula; others think the Ptolemies are enough to explain it.
views.J: Jewish tradition kept the Torah's ban on images (Exodus 20:4) and on naming other gods (Exodus 23:13), a rule that 14:27 seems to echo. Philo, in the same city, condemns the worship of Egypt's animals and of the heavens (On the Decalogue 52–80).

deep.h: How idolatry began, and what it leads to
deep.b: The writer's order is deliberate. First, the idea (14:12): idols are a human invention, not there "at the start" and not there "forever" (14:13). Then two ways they came about: private grief turned into a household rite (14:15), and public flattery of distant kings turned into worship (14:17–20). Then the giving of "the Name that can be shared with no one" to wood and stone (14:21). Last, the results: wrong ideas about God lead to wrong lives, from secret rites and violence to broken marriages and perjury (14:22–31). The chain from false worship to moral collapse is the same one Paul uses in Romans 1:21–32.

echoes: Genesis 6:4; Genesis 7:23; Exodus 20:4; Exodus 23:13; Deuteronomy 21:23; Isaiah 42:8; Isaiah 43:16; Jeremiah 6:14; Daniel 3:1–7; Romans 1:21–32; 1 Corinthians 10:19–20; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20; Revelation 13:14–15

settings.what: A prayer in the middle of the satire: God's providence at sea
settings.why: To set God's real care for sailors, and for Noah's raft, against the sailor's prayer to a wooden idol, and so to show who actually saves.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. Alexandria was a great port; sea travel, shipwreck and sailors' gods were part of everyday life there.
views: The prayer is a statement of God's providence over all human work.
Christian readers found in the raft and the "blessed wood" a figure of the church and the cross.

title: But we are yours
sum: After the catalog of vices, the speaker turns back to God: "But you, our God, are kind and true", slow to anger and ruling all with mercy (15:1). Israel belongs to him; even if they sin they are his, and knowing this they will not sin; to know him is the root of immortality (15:2–3). Israel was not fooled by painted images (15:4–6).

Then the satire resumes with the potter. From the same clay he makes useful pots and a useless god, though he was himself made from earth and must soon give back the soul lent to him (15:7–13). Worst of all were Egypt's idols: all the idols of the nations, and animals besides, creatures without beauty, left out of God's praise and blessing (15:14–19). This brings the digression back to Egypt, ready for the second contrast in chapter 16.
readings: Read as confession of faith
Verses 1–3 echo Exodus 34:6 and are one of the book's short prayers of Israel's faith: God is merciful, Israel is his, knowing him is life.
Read beside Romans 2 and 9
Paul seems to know this chapter twice: the confidence of 15:2 is the kind he challenges in Romans 2, and the potter of 15:7 reappears in Romans 9:21, turned to a different point.

views.C: Catholic readers see in 15:1–3 the faith of Israel before Christ: God's mercy (Exodus 34:6), his choosing of a people, and knowledge of God as the root of eternal life (compare John 17:3).
views.O: Orthodox readers hear 15:1, "kind and true, slow to anger", in the words of their own liturgy, which often praises God as merciful and loving to humankind, and read 15:11 with Genesis 2:7 on the soul as God's gift.
views.P: Many Protestant commentators on Romans think Paul has 15:2, "Even if we sin, we are yours", in view when he warns those who judge others while doing the same things (Romans 2:1–4, 17–24). Others think the verse expresses ordinary covenant trust and is not complacent at all.
views.H: Egyptian religion's animal cults were ancient and flourished in Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, which suits a writer in Alexandria. Most scholars think the potter of 15:7 and Paul's potter of Romans 9:21 are related, since they share several Greek words.
views.J: The confidence that Israel belongs to God even when it sins (15:2) is the prophets' (Jeremiah 3:22; Hosea 14:1–4) and later rabbinic teaching's too. The mockery of idols with useless eyes, ears and feet comes from Psalm 115 and Psalm 135.

echoes: Genesis 1:22; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Exodus 34:6; Psalm 115:4–8; Psalm 135:15–17; Isaiah 45:9; Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18:6; Luke 12:20; John 17:3; Romans 2:1–4; Romans 9:20–21

settings.when: right after the catalog of vices (14:22–31)
settings.why: To set Israel's God and Israel's worship against the idolatry just described, and to remind Israel that belonging to God is a reason not to sin.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. The prayer gave them words to say who they were among their neighbors: a people that belongs to the one God and refuses images.
views: Many read it as covenant trust, like the prophets' promises.
Some, reading it with Romans 2, hear a risky sense of being safe from judgment.

settings.when: closing the digression on idols and returning to the Exodus
settings.why: To show that Egypt, the oppressor, was the most foolish of all, worshiping every idol and the lowest animals, and so to prepare the second contrast (16:1–4), where animals feed Israel.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last centuries before Jesus or in his lifetime: a large community living as a minority among Egyptians, who honored sacred animals, and Greeks, who honored statues and their kings. They lived among the very animal cults the passage mocks.
views: The passage is pointed polemic against Egyptian religion.
It is also the bridge back to the Exodus contrasts.
